analytic.title: Real-Time Scheduling and Analysis of OpenMP Task Systems with Tied Tasks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: OpenMP is a promising framework for developing parallel real-time software on multi-cores. Although similar to the DAG task model, OpenMP task systems are significantly more difficult to analyze due to constraints posed by the OpenMP specification. An important feature in OpenMP is tied tasks, which must execute on the same thread during the whole life cycle. Although tied tasks enjoy benefits in simplicity and efficiency, it was considered to be not suitable to real-time systems due to its complex behavior. In this paper, we study the realtime scheduling and analysis of OpenMP task systems with tied tasks. First, we show that under the existing scheduling algorithms in OpenMP, tied tasks indeed may lead to extremely bad timing behaviors where the parallel workload is sequentially executed completely. To solve this problem, we proposed a new scheduling algorithm and developed two response time bounds for it, with different trade-off between simplicity and analysis precision. Experiments with both randomly generated OpenMP task systems and realistic OpenMP programs show that the response time bounds obtained by our approach for tied task systems are very close to that of untied tasks.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Multi-cores are more and more widely used in real-time systems to meet the rapidly increasing requirements in high performance and low power consumption. To fully utilize the computation power of multi-core processors, software must be parallelized. OpenMP [1] is a popular parallel programming framework, which is not only widely used in general and high-performance computing, but also has drawn increasing interests in embedded and real-time computing [2]- [5].

A common way to model parallel workload is using Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAG). Since version 4.0, OpenMP supports explicit tasks, the execution semantics of which are closely related to the DAG model. This motivates much theoretical work on real-time scheduling and analysis of DAG task models [5]- [12]. However, the OpenMP language framework poses many constraints to the workload model and runtime scheduling behavior, which cannot be fully captured by the DAG task model. Therefore, existing results with DAG models are not directly applicable to realistic OpenMP task systems.

An important feature in OpenMP task systems is introduced by the tied keyword, which enforces a task (which includes several vertices in a DAG) to execute on the same thread during its life cycle. The tied tasks enjoy the following benefits [1], [4]: (1) tied task precludes migrations among threads, which simplifies the implementation of the scheduling algorithm and reduces context switch cost; (2) tied tasks may prevent deadlocks in the presence of critical sections in many cases. In OpenMP, all tasks are tied by default, unless an untied keyword is explicitly placed when the task is created.

However, tied tasks and related constraints in OpenMP bring significant challenges. [4] showed that the scheduling algorithms in OpenMP are work-conserving if all tasks are untied, and thus the classical response time bound [13] is still applicable. However, when there are tied tasks, the scheduling algorithms in OpenMP are not work-conserving, and consequently "timing analysis for tied tasks, besides being conceptually very difficult to achieve, would require to address sources of inherent complexity that would lead to unacceptably pessimistic response-time bounds" [4]. So far, the problem of scheduling OpenMP task systems containing tied tasks with guaranteed response time bounds is open.

In this paper, we address the above open problem. First, we show that under existing algorithms in OpenMP, tied tasks not only make the analysis difficult, but indeed may lead to extremely bad timing behavior: the parallel workload is almost completely tied to a single thread, and thus has to be executed sequentially. Therefore, existing algorithms in OpenMP are indeed not suitable to real-time systems where guaranteed response time bounds are required. To solve this problem, we propose a new algorithm to schedule OpenMP task systems, which at runtime uses simple rules to avoid tying too much workload to the same thread. Then we developed two response time bounds for the new algorithm, with different trade-off between simplicity (efficiency) and analysis precision.

We conduct experiments with both randomly generated task systems and realistic OpenMP programs to evaluate our proposed scheduling algorithm and analysis techniques. Experiment results show that in most cases the response time bounds obtained by our approach, (especially the second response time analysis) for tied task systems are very close to that of untied tasks, which suggests that tied tasks can also be used in OpenMP-based real-time systems.

div.head: II. OVERVIEW OF OPENMP PROGRAMS
div.p: This paper considers OpenMP 3.0 or higher version, which supports the task directive. For simplicity, we only focus on explicity OpenMP tasks, which are annotated by the task directive. The implicity OpenMP tasks which are related to work-sharing directives are out of the scope of this paper.

div.head: A. OpenMP Threads
div.p: An OpenMP program starts with a parallel directive (e.g., Line 1 in List 1), which constructs the associated parallel region including all code enclosed in a pair of the brackets following the parallel directive (e.g., Lines 2 to 23 in List 1). The parallel directive creates a team of m OpenMP threads (m being specified with the num_threads clause). An OpenMP thread is an execution entity (e.g., a thread in the underlying OS) which is able to execute the computation within the parallel region. Similar to previous work [3], [4], each thread is assumed to exclusively execute on a dedicated core. Therefore, in the rest of this paper, the concept of "thread" is equivalent to a physical processing core.

div.head: B. OpenMP Tasks
div.p: The code in the parallel region consists of a set of independent parallel units, called OpenMP tasks. In the rest of the paper, the term "task" refers an OpenMP task. A task is annotated by the task directive (e.g., τ 2 , Line 4 at List 1). The body of a task includes the codes that are enclosed in the brackets following the task directive (e.g., the code in Lines 5, 6, 17, 18, 20, 21 and 22 belongs to task τ 2 ).

If the task directive of a task τ is enclosed in the body of another task τ , then τ is a child of τ , and τ is the parent of τ . Two tasks that share the same parent are siblings. Moreover, a task τ is a descendant of τ if τ is a child or grandchild of τ , and in this case, τ is the ancestor of τ . For example, in List. 1, the task τ 2 is a child of task τ 1 . Tasks τ 4 , τ 5 and τ 6 are siblings, since they share the common parent τ 3 . Task τ 4 is a descendant of τ 1 . Task τ 2 is an ancestor of τ 4 .

div.head: C. Task Synchronization
div.p: We consider two most widely used synchronization mechanisms in OpenMP:

• taskwait. A task can synchronize with its children via taskwait clauses. When encountering taskwait, the parent task is blocked until all of its children (but not grandchildren) created beforehand have been finished. • depend. Sibling tasks synchronize with each other via depend clauses. If a task has an in dependence on a variable, it cannot start execution until all its previously created siblings with out or inout dependences on the same variable are completed. If a task has an out or inout on a variable, it cannot start execution until all its previously created siblings with in, out or inout dependences on the same variable are completed. In List 1, task τ 2 synchronizes with τ 3 , τ 7 by taskwait: τ 2 cannot be executed until τ 3 and τ 7 are completed. τ 4 , τ 5 and τ 6 synchronize with each other by depend: τ 5 waits for the completion of τ 4 , and τ 6 waits for τ 4 and τ 5 .

div.head: D. Runtime Constraints
div.p: At runtime, tasks are scheduled to execute on threads. In OpenMP, a feasible schedule fulfills the following constraints.

Task Scheduling Points (TSP). The body of a task is sequentially executed and can only be interrupted at TSP. A TSP occurs upon task creation and completion, as well as synchronization points such as taskwait directives 1 . TSPs divide a program into several parts (e.g., part10 in List 1), and a TSP exists between any two adjacent parts. In other words, the execution of each part is non-preemptive.

Tied Tasks. In OpenMP, a task is either tied or untied. A tied task forces the code in its body to be executed on the same thread. In particular, if the execution of a tied task is interrupted, later it must be resumed on the same thread. In contrast, an untied task can be executed on different threads. In particular, when an untied task is resumed, it can be executed on any idle thread. By default, OpenMP tasks are tied, unless explicitly specified as untied.

Task Scheduling Constraint (TSC). OpenMP enforces the task scheduling constraint [1]: "In order to start the execution of a new tied task, the new task must be a descendant of every task that is currently tied on the same thread." Details about this constraint will be introduced in Section III-B.

div.head: A. Graph Model of OpenMP Task Systems
div.p: We consider an OpenMP task system T consisting of n tasks {τ 1 , • • • , τ n }, and each task is either tied or untied. A task τ i contains a set of sequentially ordered parts {P i0 , P i1 , • • • }. The task system T can be represented as a DAG 2 G = (V, E), where V represents the set of vertices, and E represents the set of edges. A vertex v ix in V corresponds to the x-th part P ix of task τ i and is associated with a worst-case computation time C ix . We distinguish two types of vertices, Taskwait vertices and others, i.e., V = V T W ∪ V N .

• Taskwait Vertices (V T W ): the vertices correspond to the parts that immediately follow taskwait clauses, e.g., part23 in List. 1. In OpenMP, the taskwait clause cannot appear at the beginning of the body of a task, so the first vertex of a task must not be a taskwait vertex. • Normal Vertices (V N ): all the other vertices except those in V T W are of this type. Edge (v ix , v jz ) in E denotes the precedence constraint between vertices v ix and v jz . There are three types of edges in a DAG, i.e., E = E 1 ∪ E 2 ∪ E 3 :

• Control Flow Edges (E 1 ), denoted by dotted-line arrows in Fig. 1, model the control flow dependencies within a task. For any task τ i , there is a control flow edge between its vertices v ix and v i,x+1 (x = 0, 1, • • • ). • Task Creation Edges (E 2 ), denoted by dashed-line arrows. A parent task points its child tasks via this type of edges. In Fig. 1, (v 31 , v 50 ) is a task creation edge. An edge of this type must comply with the following rule:

div.head: B. OpenMP Runtime Model
div.p: Given a task graph G = (V, E) and a team of threads S = {s 1 , • • • , s m }, a schedule is to assign tasks to threads, so that each vertex of V is executed until completion.
For each vertex v ix ∈ V , we use the following notations:
• b ix : the time when v ix begins its execution.
• f ix : the time when v ix completes its execution.
• e ix : the time when v ix becomes eligible, which is the latest finishing time among all the predecessors of v ix :
div.formula: e ix = max{f jz |∀(v jz , v ix ) ∈ E}.
div.p: The target of this work is to compute an upper bound of the response time R of an OpenMP task system G = (V, E): As introduced in Section II-D, at runtime the scheduling of OpenMP tasks must fulfill several constraints. The first constraint requires that a part must execute until completion once started. Therefore, in our graph-based OpenMP task model, the execution of each vertex is non-preemptive (note that the execution of a task may be preempted or suspended at the boundary of two vertices). The second constraint requires that a tied task, once started execution on one thread, cannot migrate to another. Therefore, in our model, all the vertices of a task annotated as tied must be executed by the same thread.
div.formula: R = max{f ix |v ix ∈ V } We say a vertex is delayed if b ix > e ix ,
div.p: The third constraint, namely the Task Scheduling Constraint (TSC), is a bit complicated. Its formal statement within our model is as follows: TSC: At time t, the first vertex v i0 of a tied task τ i can be executed by thread

div.p: TSC enforces that a new tied task τ i can be executed by thread s k at time t only if τ i is the descendant of all active tasks tied to s k before t. Note that as a special case of the above condition, if Γ k (t) = ∅, τ i can be executed by s k .

At time t 1 , the currently tied task set of s 1 is Γ 1 (t 1 ) = {τ 3 }, and the tasks τ 4 and τ 5 are both eligible at time t 1 since e 40 = f 12 < t 1 and e 50 = f 11 < t 1 . Under TSC, τ 5 can be executed by s 1 and τ 4 is delayed since τ 5 is the child of τ 3 , but τ 4 is not.

div.head: IV. PROBLEMS WITH EXISTING SCHEDULING POLICIES
div.p: Most OpenMP implementations support two scheduling policies: Work First Scheduling (WFS) [14] and Breadth First Scheduling (BFS) [15]. WFS prefers to execute newly created tasks, while BFS tends to execute tasks that have been tied on the thread. As pointed by [16] WFS is not suitable to schedule systems with tied tasks , since it completely sequentializes the execution of task when nested parallelism (found, for example, in programs that use recursion) is adopted. Therefore, in the remaining of this paper we focus on BFS.

The pseudo-code of BFS is shown in Alg. 1. The algorithm is invoked when a vertex v ix (of τ i ) completes execution. If τ i has been tied to thread s k and its immediate successor v i,x+1 is eligible (line 1), then the scheduler executes v i,x+1 on s k (line 2). After that, if there is any vertex v jz (of τ j ) that is eligible but has not been executed (Line 3), the scheduler finds an idle thread s h to execute it. The three if conditions (line 4, 6 and 8) are disjoint, so only one of three cases will be taken. If none of these conditions are met, v jz will not be executed.
Serrano et al. [4] showed that BFS is work-conserving when scheduling untied task, based on which it was proved that the classical response time bound [13] for DAG still holds:
div.formula: R ≤ len(G) + vol(G) -len(G) m (1
div.p: where len(G) is the length of critical path in DAG G, and vol(G) is the total worst-case computation time of all the vertices in G, and m is the number of threads. Unfortunately, BFS is not work-conserving and the bound in (1) is not applicable when there are tied tasks. Nevertheless, BFS is a better choice for scheduling tied tasks in practice than WFS: BFS does not force the thread to suspend the parent task for executing the new child task, but has a better chance to distribute tied tasks to different threads. However, it leaves an open problem in [4] about how to bound the response time of OpenMP application with tied task under BFS. We use the example in Fig. 3 to show that in the extreme case BFS may perform as bad as WFS, i.e., BFS may also execute the parallel workload sequentially. The task system contains 3m-1 tied tasks. Each task τ 3i (i = 1, • • • , m-1) has a "heavy" vertex v 3i,2 , and the last task τ 3m-1 also has a "heavy" vertex v 3m-1,1 . All the other vertices are "light" vertices. The heavy vertices (marked red in Fig. 3) have WCET l. The light vertices' WCETs are much smaller than l. The WCETs of light vertices are constructed so that the schedule under BFS is shown in Fig. 4. At any time when a task τ 3i is created (i = 2, • • • , m-1), s m is the only one idle thread. Moreover, at that time the active tied tasks on s m are τ 3 ,• • • ,τ 3i-3 , which are the ancestor of τ 3i . According to Line 8 of Alg. 1, τ 3i is executed by s m . On the other hand, at any time when a task τ 3i+1 is created, s i is the only idle thread, which has no active tied task at that time. Therefore, τ 3i+1 is executed by s i according to Line 8 of Alg. 1. Consequently, the schedule has two phases. In the first phase, all the heavy tasks are tied to thread s m . In the second phase, s m executes the heavy vertices sequentially, and all the other threads are idle. When the execution time of all the light vertices approaches 0, the response time of this OpenMP application approaches its total workload vol(G) = ml.

In this example, we observe that under BFS a task (e.g., τ 3i ) newly tied on a thread (e.g., s m ) will block the tasks (e.g., τ 3 , • • •, τ 3i-3 ) that have been tied on the same thread, even if this newly tied task is their descendant. This, in the worst case, leads to a sequential executions of workload that could execute in parallel. This motivates us to design a new scheduling policy in the next section to avoid this kind of blocking and eventually improve the worst-case response time.

div.head: V. NEW SCHEDULING POLICY: BFS *
div.p: In this section, we develop a new scheduling policy BFS * to mitigate the resource waste problem caused by tied tasks. BFS * is similar to BFS in the sense of first executing currently tied tasks, but uses an enhanced version of TSC as follows:
E-TSC: For any vertex vix that is the first vertex of a tied task or which belongs to a untied task τi, sk can execute

Recall that j (t) is the currently suspended vertex of τ j . In TSC, a tied task is allowed to execute on s k as long as it is the descendant of all the tasks already tied to s k . The admission control in E-TSC is more conservative. Intuitively, it does not allow a vertex v ix to execute on s k unless really necessary (in the sense that the continuation of the suspended tasks tied to s k depends on v ix ).

div.p: The pseudo-code of BFS * is presented in Alg. 2, where we use E-TSC to replace TSC. The key point of E-TSC and BFS * is to be able to guarantee the following properties, based on which the response time can be well bounded.

The first one is about delayed vertices. Recall that a vertex v ix is delayed if it begins its execution later than the time it becomes eligible, i.e., b ix > e ix . The following lemma states that once a tied task starts execution, none of its vertices can be delayed in the future. Lemma 3. Given a tied task τ i , v ix can be delayed under BFS * only if v ix is the first vertex of τ i .

Proof. We prove the lemma by contradiction, assuming the vertex v ix is not the first vertex of a tied task τ i and is delayed at t, i.e., . e ix ≤ t < b ix . Since v ix is not the first vertex of τ i and is eligible at t, τ i must have been tied to some thread s k , i.e., τ i ∈ Γ k (t). We consider two cases.
(1) s k is idle at t. Since v ix is eligible at t, v ix can be executed by s k at t according to Line 4 of Alg. 2, which leads to a contradiction.
(2) s k is busy at t. Suppose that s k is executing task τ j at t. We first consider the case that τ j is tied.

• b j0 < b i0 . τ j is active at t, so it is also active at b i0 , i.e., τ j ∈ Γ k (b i0 ). At b i0 , the assignment of v i0 to s k implies that τ i is a descendant of τ j , and v i0 is a predecessor of j (b i0 ) according to Line 7 of Alg. 2. By Lem. 1, the last vertex of τ i is the predecessor of j (b i0 ) of τ j . Therefore, once τ j is preempted by τ i , it cannot be executed until τ i is completed. It contradicts to the assumption that τ j is being executed at a time t when the vertex of τ i is delayed (which implies that τ i is unfinished at t).

By Lem. 1, the last vertex of τ j is a predecessor of i (b j0 ). Moreover, since b j0 ≤ t, we know i (b j0 ) is either i (t) or i (t)'s predecessor. Therefore, the last vertex of τ j is a predecessor of i (t).

As i (t) = v ix , we can conclude that the last vertex of τ j is a predecessor of v ix . Therefore, v ix is not eligible until τ j is completed. This contradicts to the assumption that v ix is eligible at t and τ j is unfinished at t. Then we consider the case that τ j is untied, and assume that a vertex v jz of τ j is executed by s k at t. We know that v jz starts after the completion of v i,x-1 . Since τ i ∈ Γ k (b jz ) and the suspended vertex of τ i at b jz is v ix , the assignment of v jz to s k must fulfill the condition that τ j is a descendant of τ i and that v jz is a predecessor of v ix of τ i . By Lem. 1, the last vertex of τ j is a predecessor of v ix . Therefore, v ix cannot be eligible until τ j is finished. It contradicts to the assumption that v ix is eligible at t and τ j is unfinished at t.
All the above cases lead to contradictions. Proved.

The second property of BFS * is about suspended tasks. Recall that a tied task τ i ∈ Γ k (t) is suspended at time t if s k does not execute τ i at that time (Def. 3). Lemma 4. A tied task can only be suspended at its taskwait vertices.

Proof. We prove by contradiction, assuming that at t a tied task τ i is suspended, and the suspended vertex v ix is not a taskwait vertex, i.e., only edge (v i,x-1 , v ix ) points to v ix . In this case, v ix becomes eligible once v i,x-1 is completed, i.e., e ix = f i,x-1 . Since τ i is suspended at t, and the suspended vertex i (t) = v ix , we know v i,x-1 is completed before or at t, and v ix starts after t, i.e., e ix (= f i,x-1 ) ≤ t < b ix . Therefore, v ix (which is not the first vertex of τ i ) is delayed at t, which contradicts to Lem. 3.

div.head: VII. EVALUATION
div.p: This section evaluates our response time bounds for BFS * with both randomly generated task sets and realistic OpenMP programs. For each task set, we calculate the bounds in (12), denoted by R 1 , and (25), denoted by R 2 , and then compare them with the response time bound in (1) for BFS [4], denoted by R 0 , assuming all the tasks are untied. R 1 and R 2 are normalized with respect to R 0 .

div.head: A. Randomly Generated Tasks
div.p: We generate the DAG G with n tasks {τ 1 , • • • , τ n }, and for any task τ j (j ∈ [2, n]), randomly assign a task τ i (i ∈ [1, j -1)) to be the parent of τ j . We consider three types of tasks with parameter ranges given in Table I. For each task, one of these types is randomly selected. Then the task parameters are randomly chosen from the corresponding intervals. For any parent task τ i , a vertex v ix of τ i is a taskwait vertex with p wait probability if a predecessor of v ix has an outgoing task creation edge. For any task τ i , the last vertex of τ i points to one of its siblings created after τ i through depend edges with p dep probability. All the tasks are set to be tied. For each data point, 100 random experiments have been run.

We conduct experiments with different combinations of parameters in Fig. 5 and6. In The response time bound R 2 is consistently close to the baseline bound R 0 with different parameter settings. However, the difference between R 1 and R 0 is much larger. As shown in Fig. 5(a), the bounds R 1 and R 2 decrease as the number of threads increases. Moreover, as shown in Fig. 5(c) and Fig. 6(a), the bounds increase as the depth dep(G) and the probability p wait increase, while the growth of R 2 is very slow. In Fig. 5(b), the bound R 1 tends to increase as the number of tasks increases. In Fig. 6(b), both of the bounds do not change significantly as the probability p dep increases.

div.head: B. Realistic Benchmarks
div.p: We collect 18 OpenMP programs based on C language from several benchmarks (See in Table. II) and transform them to DAGs by a tool, called ompTG [17]. Columns 3-7 show whether the applications contain a certain structure feature, where T stands for tied tasks, W stands for taskwait clauses, D stands for depend clauses. shown in Table II, these programs have small depths, which are 1 or 2. The last four programs (from st to fb) are all from the BOTS benchmark, which contain recursive functions. The depths of these programs are large. Especially, the depth of fib equals 9. The three bounds of the first seven programs (marked with * ) are the same. For each of the next seven programs (from br to sn), the response time bounds R 1 and R 2 are bn * pd * su * sn * ad * fm * sa * br nd op pg th su sn st ft ns fb 0 very close to the baseline bound R 0 . For each of the last four programs, the difference between the response time bound R 2 and R 0 remains an acceptable bound, i.e, the largest gap is no more than 0.5 (with fb). However, the difference between R 1 and R 0 becomes very large due to the large depths.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: OpenMP is a popular parallel programming framework in general-purpose/high-performance computing, and is also promising for real-time computing. Previous work has studied the timing analysis of OpenMP task systems, but existing techniques cannot handle tied tasks. In this paper we propose a new algorithm to schedule OpenMP task systems with tied tasks, and derive response time bounds under the new scheduling algorithm.

An OpenMP task system should be modeled as a DAG with conditional branching since the fork-join structures may be nested with branching structures (e.g., the if-else structure). Including conditional branching semantics will make the model rather complicated. For presentation simplicity, we assume DAGs without conditional branching to focus on the main point of this paper: how to handle tied tasks in scheduling and analysis. The results of this paper can be extended to include conditional branching structures.

div.head: APPENDIX A: COMPUTING dep(G)
div.p: To calculate dep(G), we construct a task tree F as follows. For any tasks τ i and τ j , there is an edge (τ j , τ i ) if τ j → τ i . In F, each path corresponds to a depended sequence. Thus, computing dep(G) is equal to find a path in F containing the maximum number of tied non-leaves (since the leaf task in F can only be the first task of a depended sequence). This can be solved by the following recursive functions. For any leaf τ i ∈ F, let N tied (τ i ) = 0, and for any non-leaf τ i ∈ F:
where N tied (τ i ) is the maximum number of tied non-leaves contained in the path of F that ends at τ i . Let dep(G) = max{N tied (τ i )|τ i ∈ F}, this terminates within O(n) time.

div.head: APPENDIX B: COMPUTING len(λ ix )
div.p: We know that the last vertex of path λ ix is the predecessor of a taskwait vertex v ix of τ i , and λ ix does not travel any vertex of τ i . From Rule E3.1, the taskwait vertex v ix of τ i can only be connected by the vertex in τ i or the vertex in the child of τ i . Moreover, according to Lem. 14, there is no path that connects a non-descendant of τ i to the descendant of τ i and without travelling any vertex in τ i . Thus, λ ix can only travel the descendants of τ i .
By D ix we denote the subgraph consisting of the descendant τ j of τ i such that v ix is reachable from the vertex of τ j . More formally, D ix is defined as follows.
Any task τ j ∈ D ix if:

• τ j is a depended task of τ i which joins to v ix ; or • τ j is a depended task of a task in D ix . For any τ j and τ l in D ix , all the edges between τ j and τ l belong to D ix . Calculating len(λ ix ) equals finding the longest path in D ix . This is calculated by the following recursion:
where L(v jz ) is the length of the longest path in D ix with the starting vertex v jz . Let len(λ ix ) = max{L(v jz )|v jz ∈ D ix }, this calculation is terminated within O(|E|) time.

div.head: APPENDIX C: CALCULATION OF len v (G)
div.p: Given the graph G with virtual computation times, the virtual length of G can be recursively computed as follows. Denote by G ix the subgraph consisting of vertices reachable from v ix . The virtual length of G ix is calculated by: We first introduce the following auxiliary lemma. Lemma 14. If task τ is a descendant of task τ and τ is not a descendant of τ , there is no edge between τ and τ .
Proof. The lemma is proved by enumerating all the three types of edges E 1 , E 2 and E 3 : none of them can connect a descendant and a non-descendant of a task.

The proof of Lem. 1. It is sufficient to prove that any path from v to v must travel the last vertex of τ . We prove this by contradiction, assuming there is a path λ from v to v that does not travel through the last vertex of τ . Let u be the first vertex of λ such that u belongs to neither τ nor a descendant of τ . Therefore, the immediate predecessor u of u in λ belongs to either τ or a descendant of τ . Since u belongs to a task that is not a descendant of τ , and there is an edge between u and u, u must not belong to a descendant of τ according to Lem. 14. Therefore, u must belong to τ . By now, we can conclude that the source vertex u of (u , u) belongs to τ , and the destination vertex u of (u , u) belongs to a non-descendant of τ . Since only the edge in E 3 can connect a task to another task that is not its descendant, we know (u , u) ∈ E 3 . According to Rule E3.1 and Rule E3.2, we know u must be the last vertex of τ . Therefore, λ travels through the last vertex of τ , which contradicts to the assumption.

The proof of Lem. 2. It is sufficient to prove that any path from v to v must travel through the first vertex of τ . We prove it by contradiction, assuming there is a path λ from v to v that does not travel through the first vertex of τ . Let u be the last vertex of λ which belongs to neither τ nor the descendant of τ . Therefore, the immediate successor u of u in λ belongs to either τ or a descendant of τ . Since u belongs to a nondescendant of τ and there is an edge (u , u), u must not belong to any descendant of τ according to Lem. 14. Therefore, u must belong to τ . By now, we know the source vertex u of (u , u) belongs to a non-descendant of τ , and the destination vertex u of (u , u) belongs to τ . Since only the task creation edge in E 2 or the depend edge can connect a non-descendant of τ to τ , we know that (u , u) is either a task creation edge or a depend edge. According to Rule E2 and Rule E3.2, u is the first vertex of τ . Therefore, λ also travels through the first vertex of τ , which contradicts the assumption.
